notes: AG reference on attempted robbery with air pistol; wholly exceptional depressive illness and post-sentence progress justify refusing leave.

enrichment.short_title: AG reference refused over community order for post office robbery with air pistol
key_facts: A 20-year-old offender attempted to rob a local sub-post office in Wythenshawe with a .177 air pistol resembling a handgun; the sub-postmaster raised the alarm and nothing was stolen.
At sentencing he was suffering from a depressive illness complicated by alcohol dependency, and psychiatric evidence indicated he had expected and wanted to be caught.
His Honour Judge Lyon imposed a three-year community rehabilitation order with psychiatric counselling instead of the custodial sentence normally expected for robbery involving a firearm.
The Attorney General sought leave to refer the sentence as unduly lenient, relying on authorities such as Attorney General's Reference No 2 of 1989 and Duffy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference seeking leave to refer an unduly lenient sentence for attempted robbery and possession of a firearm while committing an indictable offence.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to refer refused; the sentencing judge's exceptional community rehabilitation order upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Although robbery with a firearm ordinarily requires a substantial custodial sentence for deterrence and protection of small businesses, an experienced sentencer may in wholly exceptional circumstances depart where the offender's mental condition at the time of the offence justifies mercy; sentencing is an art rather than a mechanical exercise and leniency is not in itself a vice.
legal_issues: Whether the sentence for attempted robbery with an air pistol was unduly lenient
Whether wholly exceptional circumstances justified a non-custodial disposal
Whether post-sentence probation reports should be taken into account on an AG reference
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference No 2 of 1989 (Darren Major) (1989) 11 Cr.App.R (S) 481
Attorney General's Reference No 83 of 2001 (Fidler) [2002] 1 Cr.App.R (S) 588
Attorney General's Reference No 4 of 1989, 90 Cr.App.R 366

confidence.notes: Facts, sentence, psychiatric context, and refusal of leave are explicit. Post-sentence burglary was noted but did not alter the outcome.

notes: Complex music producer and publishing dispute; mixed findings on copyright, accounting, and breach of implied producer obligations.

enrichment.short_title: Music producer's dispute with publisher over exclusive work, copyright and royalties
key_facts: Mark Taylor, a successful record producer and songwriter, entered into oral producer and written publishing agreements with Rive Droite Music Ltd from 1995, renewed in 1998.
He ceased working for RDM at the end of November 2000 and thereafter worked for Brian Rawling Productions Ltd.
RDM claimed breach of exclusive obligations, copyright infringement in songs including Hero and Love to See You Cry, failure to exploit Follow Your Heart, and incorrect royalty accounting.
Mr Taylor contended the 1998 publishing agreement was for two years, that he was not bound exclusively, and that RDM had misapplied the cover clause and deductions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial on breach of producer and publishing agreements, copyright infringement, rectification, and unlawful interference claims.
enrichment.outcome: Mixed judgment: publishing term held two years with no rectification; RDM estopped from minimum commitment and failed to exploit Follow Your Heart; Taylor infringed literary/musical copyright in Hero and Love to See You Cry but not sound recordings; producer services not exclusive but Taylor breached implied obligation over Cher project; limited success on unlawful interference over Hall and Oates files.
enrichment.ratio: On the agreed issues, the 1998 publishing agreement ran for two years and could not be rectified to three; RDM was estopped from enforcing the minimum song commitment; producer services were not exclusive but an implied term required Taylor not to prevent RDM securing agreed projects; copyright in specified song versions as at 1 December 2000 was infringed though sound recording copyright was not; RDM's accounting deductions were limited to session musicians and a notional tape cost.
legal_issues: Construction and rectification of the 1998 publishing agreement term
Whether the producer agreement imposed exclusive services
Copyright infringement in Hero and Love to See You Cry
Operation of the cover clause and minimum commitment
Proper deductions and timing of producer royalty accounts
Unlawful interference with RDM's business

notes: Restrictive covenant appeal on roadway access to adjoining development; Neuberger LJ's construction analysis is detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Restrictive covenant breach over roadway access to adjoining housing development
key_facts: A 1964 conveyance of No 28 Ox Lane, Harpenden imposed covenants restricting use to a single two-storey private dwelling and private residence only.
Jarvis Homes contracted to redevelop No 28 and proposed a metalled roadway through the garden to serve a ten-house development on adjoining land.
The deputy judge held construction and use of the roadway would not breach clause 2(b) of the covenant.
Neighbouring owners Mr and Mrs Marshall appealed, arguing the roadway and lamp-posts would breach the covenant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a deputy High Court judge on the interpretation and breach of restrictive covenants in a 1964 conveyance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; use of part of No 28 as a roadway for access to the adjoining development would breach clause 2(b), and erection of lamp-posts on No 28 would breach clause 2(a).
enrichment.ratio: The words 'the same as a private residence only' in clause 2(b) apply to the land and all parts of it, not merely buildings; granting rights of way to occupiers of adjoining houses would involve use inconsistent with private residence only and breach the covenant; clause 2(a) prohibits erection of lamp-posts other than one dwelling house with necessary outbuildings and garage, though construction of the roadway itself is primarily governed by use under clause 2(b).
legal_issues: Construction of 'private residence only' in clause 2(b)
Whether a roadway serving an adjoining development breaches the covenant
Whether third-party use via rights of way avoids covenant liability
Whether lamp-posts breach clause 2(a)
Whether construction works themselves breach clause 2(b)

notes: Scottish intestate estate; transaction at undervalue over life policy trust; appeal dismissed with interest variation.

enrichment.short_title: Setting aside undervalue trust of life policy in Scottish bankrupt estate
key_facts: Allan Thoars, domiciled in Scotland, died intestate and insolvent on 19 September 1996 shortly after a liver transplant.
On 26 July 1996 he declared a whole life assurance policy with Skandia held on trust for Ramlort Ltd in return for payments totalling £3,000.
The judicial factor of the estate sought to set aside the declaration of trust as a transaction at an undervalue under section 339 of the Insolvency Act 1986.
The trial judge valued the policy at at least £10,000 and the consideration at nil, and ordered the trust set aside with repayment to Ramlort.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Chancery Division bankruptcy judge's order setting aside a declaration of trust over a life assurance policy.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed save that Ramlort was entitled to interest on the sums repaid; declaration of trust set aside on terms reversing the transaction.
enrichment.ratio: Where a declaration of trust over a life policy constituted a transaction at an undervalue, the appropriate remedy is to set aside the trust and restore the parties to the position they would have been in had it not been made, with Ramlort recovering its payments plus interest; the policy's value at the date of the trust is not nil merely because the assured's subsequent death might affect expectations.
legal_issues: Whether the declaration of trust was a transaction at an undervalue under section 339
How to value the life policy and consideration at the date of the trust
Whether the trust should be set aside or compensated
Entitlement to interest on sums repaid to Ramlort

confidence.notes: Core insolvency facts, valuation approach, and appeal disposition are clear. Some valuation reasoning draws on property analogies.

notes: False imprisonment appeal over PACE s.28 arrest information and excessive juvenile detention at Hillgrove Farm protest.

enrichment.short_title: Lawful arrest information under PACE but excessive detention of ten-year-old protester
key_facts: Daniel Taylor, aged ten, was arrested at an anti-vivisection protest at Hillgrove Farm on 31 May 1998 on suspicion of violent disorder at an earlier demonstration on 18 April 1998.
PC McKenzie told him at arrest he was suspected of violent disorder at Hillgrove Farm on 18 April 1998; the jury found a genuine suspicion and that holding his arm was reasonable.
The county court judge held the arrest unlawful for insufficient factual detail under section 28(3) PACE and that detention between about 20.15 and 21.21 was excessive.
Damages of £1,500 were agreed subject to approval because the claimant was a minor.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by the Chief Constable against county court findings of unlawful arrest and excessive detention following a partly jury trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: arrest held lawful as the essential legal and factual grounds were communicated; award of £1,500 set aside for false imprisonment and assault but judge entitled to find about one hour's detention unlawful with quantum to be agreed.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 28(3) PACE, read with Article 5(2) ECHR and Fox, Campbell and Hartley, an arrested person must be told in simple language the essential legal and factual grounds; stating violent disorder at a named place and date of a prior demonstration the arrestee had attended was sufficient here; whether police acted reasonably in internal communication is irrelevant; the Chief Constable failed to justify detention for about an hour before interview began.
legal_issues: Whether words spoken on arrest satisfied section 28(3) PACE
Application of Christie v Leachinsky and Fox, Campbell and Hartley principles
Whether detention before interview was excessive under PACE Code C
Appropriate damages where arrest lawful but part of detention unlawful
linked_authorities: Christie v Leachinsky [1947] AC 573
Fox, Campbell and Hartley v United Kingdom (1990) 13 EHRR 157
Abbassy v Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis [1990] 1 WLR 385
Mercer v Chief Constable of Lancashire [1991] 1 WLR 367

confidence.notes: Arrest wording, PACE analysis, and split appeal outcome are comprehensively reasoned. Damages quantum on the unlawful hour was left for agreement.

notes: Murder conviction appeal; anonymous witness rulings and summing-up challenges all rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Murder appeal dismissed over anonymous witnesses and joint enterprise shooting
key_facts: Scott was convicted of murder after a shooting outside the Duke of Wellington public house in Battersea following an earlier argument inside the pub.
The Crown case was a joint enterprise in which Scott returned with a machete and co-accused Solgy fired the fatal shot.
Prosecution witnesses Sullivan and Brown gave evidence anonymously from behind screens due to fear of reprisals.
Scott's police interview account was conceded to be a lie; Veronica Whittaker's evidence was directed to be disregarded as unreliable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against conviction after murder trial at the Central Criminal Court.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to appeal refused; all grounds including anonymous witness rulings, summing-up, joint enterprise direction, good character, jury discharge, and disclosure held unarguable.
enrichment.ratio: Anonymity and screens for terrified eyewitnesses in a gang-related shooting were a proper exercise of discretion following R v Garry Taylor and Doorson v Netherlands; a voir dire is not always required where defence tactically chose not to request one; absence of a direction to treat anonymous evidence with circumspection did not render the conviction unsafe given independent supporting evidence including the defendant's lies.
legal_issues: Whether anonymous and screened witness evidence was properly permitted
Whether the judge should have directed the jury to accept Scott's account of a telephone call
Adequacy of summing-up on joint enterprise and defence case
Whether trial should have been aborted after a witness called the defendant a troublemaker
Non-disclosure of identification parade video and immigration files

notes: Cross-border jurisdiction over sound recording masters; Brussels Regulation and conversion claims analysed at length.

enrichment.short_title: Jurisdiction over sound recording masters in Anglo-German corporate dispute
key_facts: Mazur Media Ltd, Apex Entertainment Group Ltd and German subsidiary Mazur GmbH disputed ownership of master sound recordings after a 2002 share sale and copyright assignment.
German insolvency proceedings were opened against Mazur GmbH in Hanover in 2004.
The claimants sought declarations of title, delivery up, and damages for conversion against directors and the German liquidator.
Contracts contained exclusive English jurisdiction clauses governed by English law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court applications to set aside service and stay proceedings, determining jurisdiction under the Judgments Regulation and insolvency stay issues.
enrichment.outcome: English court has exclusive jurisdiction over Apex's contractual claim against Mrs Mazur and Mazur Ltd's contractual title claim against Mazur GmbH under Article 23(1); no jurisdiction over conversion claims against most defendants; no stay of proceedings against Mazur GmbH.
enrichment.ratio: Exclusive jurisdiction clauses in the Share Sale Agreement and Assignment confer jurisdiction on contractual title and delivery-up claims; conversion claims based on detention of masters in Germany do not fall within Article 5(3) because the harmful event occurred in Germany and any English financial loss is indirect; section 130(2) Insolvency Act 1986 does not apply to foreign insolvency proceedings and forum conveniens factors cannot justify staying claims where exclusive jurisdiction exists.
legal_issues: Jurisdiction under Articles 5(3) and 23(1) of the Judgments Regulation
Whether conversion claims relate to contract so as to exclude Article 5(3)
Place of harmful event for detention of goods in Germany
Whether a contractual right to possession supports conversion
Stay of English proceedings due to German insolvency

notes: Fuel oil STS transfer quality dispute; Petronas contamination appeal dismissed, Fal Oil demurrage cross-appeal allowed.

enrichment.short_title: Fuel oil quality dispute after ship-to-ship transfer and demurrage indemnity
key_facts: Fal Oil sold cracked fuel oil to Petronas under a November 2000 contract requiring Yanbu standard quality with maximum 1% water and sediment.
The first cargo was loaded at Yanbu onto the Centaur, transferred ship-to-ship onto the Devon off Port Sudan, and discharged in Singapore/Pasir Gudang.
On discharge about 1,700 tonnes of water were found, far exceeding contractual limits, leading Petronas to reject the cargo and withhold payment.
Morison J held Petronas failed to prove excess water at the STS load point and that demurrage was an indemnity not a free-standing obligation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from a High Court trial on quality rejection and demurrage under a C&F fuel oil sale contract.
enrichment.outcome: Petronas's appeal on contamination dismissed; Fal Oil's cross-appeal on demurrage allowed; buyer must pay the cargo price and demurrage operates as indemnity for charterparty liability.
enrichment.ratio: Where the decisive issue is whether cargo at the STS transfer exceeded contractual water and sediment limits, the trial judge's evaluation of sampling and expert evidence should not be overturned unless plainly wrong; on demurrage, the contractual wording operated as an indemnity for the seller's liability under its charterparty rather than as an independent demurrage entitlement.
legal_issues: Whether Petronas proved contractual non-conformity of cargo at the STS point
Proper inference from Yanbu shore tank and vessel sampling evidence
Construction of demurrage clause as indemnity or free-standing obligation
Buyer's right to reject and withhold price

notes: AG reference on organised Birmingham heroin conspiracy; six unduly lenient sentences increased.

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient sentences increased for organised Birmingham heroin conspiracy
key_facts: Six offenders were convicted of conspiracy to supply heroin in Northfield, Birmingham between August and November 2002.
The enterprise used fortified council flats as bases, dedicated mobile phones, and open street dealing near schools and recreation areas.
Sharon McKeown and Peter Baria were at the forefront; Jason McKeown was the most prolific street dealer.
Her Honour Judge Fisher had passed sentences ranging from three to five years' imprisonment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 Criminal Justice Act 1988 against six unduly lenient sentences for conspiracy to supply heroin.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted; all six sentences quashed and increased, taking double jeopardy into account, to between four-and-a-half and eight years depending on role.
enrichment.ratio: A significant organised retail heroin conspiracy with aggravating features including young dealers and purchasers, open community dealing, use of stolen goods as payment, and children present warranted sentences at the top end of the range for retail Class A supply; five years after trial for leaders was unduly lenient compared with authorities such as Djahit, Twisse, and Davis and Chung.
legal_issues: Whether sentences for conspiracy to supply heroin were unduly lenient
Relative culpability of leaders, street dealers, and peripheral participants
Aggravating features including dealing near schools and involving juveniles
Discount for late guilty pleas and double jeopardy on reference

notes: AG reference on imitation firearm robberies; supervision order replaced with 18-month DTO.

enrichment.short_title: Supervision order replaced after unduly lenient imitation firearm robberies
key_facts: Fiona Fereday, aged 17, pleaded guilty with co-defendants to robbery, attempted robberies, and possessing an imitation firearm with intent to commit robbery in Birmingham city centre in July 2003.
She grabbed a woman at an ATM, pressed a realistic imitation handgun to her neck and abdomen, and pulled the trigger; further attempts followed within an hour.
Her Honour Judge Hindley imposed a two-year supervision order with ISSP conditions, describing it as exceptionally merciful.
Post-sentence reports showed poor compliance with supervision and further offending, limiting mitigation on reference.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 Criminal Justice Act 1988 against an unduly lenient non-custodial sentence for robbery with an imitation firearm.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; supervision order quashed and replaced with an 18-month detention and training order, with surrender ordered at Birmingham Youth Court.
enrichment.ratio: Robberies at night in a city centre using a realistic imitation firearm jabbed at victims' head, neck or abdomen, committed in quick succession, required a custodial sentence to mark gravity and deterrence; an exceptionally merciful supervision order was unduly lenient, and on reference the proper equivalent was about two-and-a-half years' detention reduced to 18 months for double jeopardy and partial completion of the order.
legal_issues: Whether a supervision order for imitation firearm robberies was unduly lenient
Aggravating features of concerted night-time city centre robberies
Effect of post-sentence breach and further offending on reference
Appropriate disposal under section 100 PCC(S)A 2000 on reference
